body.text: In short:
Forecasts show ocean temperatures off Australia's east coast will be much higher than usual over summer.
A combination of El Niño and climate change has increased the risk of marine heatwaves and coral bleaching.
What's next?
Authorities are ramping up Great Barrier Reef monitoring and preparations ahead of the warmer months.
Ocean heat off parts of Australia's east coast is set to get so severe this summer, scientists have been forced to extend one of the scales used to track marine heatwaves.

The CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology's long-range forecast shows ocean temperatures across large parts of the Queensland, New South Wales, Tasmanian and Northern Territory coasts will be about 2 degrees Celsius warmer than usual over the coming months, with a very high chance of marine heatwaves.
The grim outlook comes during a year where ocean temperatures around the world have hit record highs, with last month becoming the warmest October on record at 1.05C above average.

It has prompted concerns the Great Barrier Reef could experience its seventh mass coral bleaching event in roughly a decade, while projected warming is also posing a threat to marine ecosystems off Tasmania's east coast.
CSIRO chief research scientist Alistair Hobday said heat would accumulate across south-east Australia during December and January before pushing further north.
"For the coming months in Tasmania we're expecting to see temperatures between 2.5C and 3C above average," he said.
"Those are pushing towards the highest that we will have ever seen in this region."

While the ocean temperature outlook is a forecast and there is some uncertainty about how hot waters could eventually become, current trends suggest parts of the Coral and Tasman seas could endure the warmest conditions seen since 2016.
Climate change and El Niño double act
Ocean temperatures off Australia's coastline naturally warm over spring and summer, but there are concerns that climate change is now exacerbating this.
This could be felt most in the Tasman Sea, which has been identified as a global warming hotspot, or a region that's warming faster than the global average.
Research has found that strengthening wind systems are pushing the East Australian Current pole-wards, meaning some areas in the western Tasman Sea have warmed by more than 1C since 1980.

While the El Niño pattern typically results in cooler sea surface temperatures across much of the western Pacific Ocean, it can also increase the risk of coral bleaching because of the associated warmer, drier atmospheric conditions.

"If you've got a lot of cloud, a lot of rain, a lot of wind, that tends to mix any accumulated heat through the water column and mix it away," Bureau of Meteorology principal research scientist Claire Spillman said.
"However, if the water is really still and the sun is just beating down on it, it can warm up really quickly, particularly in those shallow areas.
"We did see widespread coral bleaching during the last two El Niño events, so in 2016 and then in 2024."
Intense outlook triggers scale change

The amount of prolonged thermal stress that corals are likely to experience is monitored through a plot known as Degree Heating Months, which measures additional ocean warmth over a three-month period.

This is important because while coral might be able to withstand a day or two of higher-than-usual temperatures, it becomes stressed and can starve if the heating is prolonged. That's when coral bleaching events occur.
This year, prolonged heat is looking so severe that scientists have extended the scale range by three degrees, which Dr Hobday said would become common practice as the planet continued to warm.

"With the underlying climate change signal, the background level of the ocean temperature will keep rising and rising, and so we will need to see increases in our scales that we use to describe warming over the next 10, 20, 30 years," Dr Hobday said.
Forecast offers early warning
This is the first time a marine heatwave outlook has been publicly available during an El Niño year, with the CSIRO and BOM launching the four-month long-range forecasts in December 2025.
It is hoped that despite the concerning forecast, the early warning will give industry a better chance to prepare, making marine ecosystems more resilient in a warming world.
Examples include ramping up surveys to document change, increasing control of crown of thorns starfish, a key coral reef predator, and testing coral clones designed to cope with warmer water.
"We are more prepared than we have been in the past for these kinds of events; it is also a stress test for the future," Dr Spillman said.
"We will see warmer summers as our climate warms and so this summer will be both a challenge and an opportunity.
"Get the monitoring out there, get the instruments in the water ahead of time so we can both monitor and test our preparedness for these kinds of summers."
The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority has now increased monitoring and preparations, pointing to what it says is "likely to be a challenging summer for the Great Barrier Reef".
Reef Authority chief scientist Roger Beeden said early preparation was critical to give corals the best chance of withstanding and recovering from marine heat stress.
"Over the past month, we've seen a rapid increase in ocean temperatures across the reef, moving from below average in early October to approaching record highs by mid-November," he said.
"We can anticipate the danger, deploy our resources strategically and reduce other pressures on reefs to give corals the best chance of surviving and recovering."
Calls for an emergency response plan
The Australian Marine Conservation Society (AMCS) said forecasting and monitoring alone were not an adequate response to the threat posed to marine environments this summer.
The group has called on Environment Minister Murray Watt to enact an emergency response plan that would treat severe bleaching as a natural disaster.
"While we welcome the Reef Authority's expanded summer preparations, it is time for management to go beyond forecasting and monitoring," campaign manager Lissa Schindler said.
"We have advance warning of potentially catastrophic damage to the reef, and emergency powers that have existed for more than 20 years. What we don't have is a plan that triggers their use.

"Locking these preparations into a formal plan would mean vulnerable reefs are protected from other pressures during stress events and recovery, and the communities who depend on the reef are supported through it."

In a statement, a spokesperson for Senator Watt said Australia already had "strong existing processes in place to prepare for and manage the impact of extreme weather events" on the Great Barrier Reef.
"This includes engagement with scientists, traditional owners and industry, as well as increased monitoring, reef protection and response preparations," the spokesperson said.
"Our focus is to protect the reef year-round and build its resilience to help it withstand and recover from disturbances.
"Australia is a world-leader in reef management and our ongoing work to reduce other local pressures helps build the reef's resilience and supports its recovery."
